Perdita’s name went unspoken, yet I had no doubt that his love for her explained his wavering intentions. And who deserved love more than my noble-hearted sister? Who had a better claim to the hand of this self-appointed king than she whose very glance was worthy of a queen of nations? She loved him as he loved her, although disappointment suppressed her passion while ambition fiercely contested his.

That evening we went together to the House. Raymond knew the coming debate would examine and settle his plans and prospects, yet he remained cheerful and unconcerned. As we entered the coffee room, a hum like ten thousand swarming beehives overwhelmed our ears. Politicians stood in clusters, their brows anxious, their voices loud or low. The aristocratic party, comprising England’s richest and most influential men, seemed calmer than the rest, since the question would be debated without their participation. Ryland and his supporters stood near the fire. A man of obscure origins, Ryland had inherited enormous wealth from his father, a manufacturer. In his youth he had witnessed the king’s abdication and the merging of the Lords and Commons into a single House. He had welcomed these advances of popular power and devoted his life to securing and extending them. Since then the landowners’ influence had increased, and at first Ryland had been pleased to watch Lord Raymond’s maneuvers draw away many supporters of his opponents. Now, however, matters were going too far. The poorer nobles welcomed the restoration of monarchy as a means of recovering their lost authority and privileges. The nearly extinguished spirit of royalty stirred again in people’s minds. Willing slaves, declaring themselves subjects, they stood ready to bow their necks beneath the yoke. A few upright, courageous spirits remained as pillars of the state, but the word republic had grown tiresome to ordinary ears. Many—whether a majority would soon be known—longed for the glitter and spectacle of royalty. Ryland rose to resist. He declared that only his tolerance had allowed this party to grow; the time for indulgence was over, and with one sweep of his arm he would clear away the cobwebs that blinded his countrymen.

Raymond’s friends greeted his arrival in the coffee room with something close to a shout. They crowded around him, counted their numbers, and explained in detail why they now expected to gain this or that member who had yet to declare his position.

After dinner the whole gang went out to search the bar for turtle eggs. They wandered about thrusting sticks into the sand, and wherever they discovered a soft patch they knelt and dug with their hands. A single hole sometimes yielded fifty or sixty eggs, round white objects slightly smaller than an English walnut. That evening they enjoyed a splendid feast of fried eggs, and another on Friday morning.

When breakfast was over they rushed whooping and capering onto the bar, pursuing one another in circles and casting off garments as they ran, until nothing remained on them. Then they carried their play far up the bar’s shallow water, pushing against the strong current, which now and again swept their legs away and added greatly to their delight. At intervals they crouched together and flung water into one another’s faces with their palms, edging closer with heads turned aside from the choking spray, until at last they seized and wrestled each other. The strongest ducked his companion, and then the whole company sank in a confusion of white arms and legs, to emerge blowing, spluttering, laughing, and catching their breath all at once.

Once thoroughly worn out, they ran ashore and sprawled upon the hot, dry sand, lying there and heaping it over themselves; presently they would dash back into the water and repeat the whole performance. At length they noticed that their bare skins did very well for flesh-coloured ‘tights’; they marked out a ring in the sand and gave a circus, complete with three clowns, since nobody would surrender that most honourable position to another.

Afterwards they brought out their marbles and played ‘knucks,’ ‘ringtaw,’ and ‘keeps’ until those diversions lost their savour. Joe and Huck then swam again, but Tom dared not follow. In kicking away his trousers he had also kicked the string of rattlesnake rattles from his ankle, and he marvelled that he had avoided cramp so long without this mysterious charm’s protection. He would not risk another swim before recovering it, and by then his companions were tired and inclined to rest. Little by little they strayed apart, grew downhearted, and began looking wistfully over the broad river at the village sleeping in the sunshine. Tom caught himself tracing ‘BECKY’ in the sand with his big toe. He scuffed it away, annoyed by his own weakness. Nevertheless, he wrote it again; he could not stop himself. Erasing it a second time, he escaped temptation by gathering the other boys together and joining them.

‘Will you play?’

‘I believe, sir,’ said the spy, turning to Mr. Lorry in his most servile manner, ‘that I can appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness. Would you ask this much younger gentleman whether a man in his position could ever justify playing the Ace he mentioned? I admit I am a spy, and that people consider the occupation shameful, though someone must do it. But this gentleman is no spy. Why should he lower himself by becoming one?’

‘I shall play my Ace in a very few minutes, Mr. Barsad,’ Carton answered for himself, glancing at his watch, ‘without the slightest regret.’

‘I would have hoped, gentlemen,’ the spy said, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the conversation, ‘that your respect for my sister—’

‘The best way I could show respect for your sister would be to rid her of her brother for good,’ said Sydney Carton.

‘You really think so, sir?’

‘My mind is entirely made up.’

The spy’s smooth manners were strangely at odds with his deliberately rough clothes, and probably with his usual behaviour. But Carton’s unreadable expression unsettled him. Carton had puzzled wiser and more honest men than he was, and now the spy’s confidence faltered and deserted him. While he struggled for an answer, Carton resumed his earlier manner of studying an imaginary hand of cards.

‘Now that I think about it, I have a strong feeling there is another good card here that I haven’t mentioned. That friend of yours, your fellow Sheep, who said he had been grazing in the country prisons—who was he?’

‘A Frenchman. You don’t know him,’ the spy answered quickly.

‘French, is he?’ Carton repeated thoughtfully. Although he echoed the word, he seemed scarcely aware of the speaker. ‘Well, perhaps he is.’

‘He certainly is,’ said the spy. ‘Though it doesn’t matter.’

‘Though it doesn’t matter,’ Carton repeated in the same absent way. ‘Though it doesn’t matter. No, it doesn’t matter. No. Still, I know that face.’

‘I doubt that. In fact, I’m sure you don’t. You can’t,’ said the spy.

‘I—can’t,’ Sydney Carton murmured, searching his memory and again toying with his glass, fortunately a small one. ‘Can’t. He spoke good French. But like a foreigner, I thought?’

‘A regional accent,’ said the spy.

‘No. A foreign one!’ Carton cried, slapping the table as understanding suddenly came. ‘Cly! In disguise, but the same man. We saw him at the Old Bailey.’

‘Now you are being hasty, sir,’ Barsad said, with a smile that pulled his hooked nose farther to one side. ‘There you have truly given me an advantage.’
